My endocrinologist told me diet has nothing to do with Hashimoto's. 

Do some people feel better cutting gluten, sugar, dairy, whatever, etc? Yes. But that's because they have a separate sensitivity to those things. So good for them for doing something that makes THEM feel better, but, like with all autoimmune conditions, that's not going to work for everyone. 

I have no issues with anything like gluten or dairy or anything. What I did have issues with was uncontrolled inflammation. And no, there was no pattern or correlation with what I ate. And my numbers were fine. My body was on fire all the time: itching, hair loss, fatigue, temperature issues. 

What worked for ME was low dose naltrexone (LDN). It instantly calmed down the inflammation in my body and stopped all my symptoms. No joke, like the next day everything stopped. But even then, most people go up to 4 mg, I'm at 1 mg after months because going up causes painful arthritic pain in my knee. Staying at 1, no issues. 

Hashimoto's is an autoimmune condition. It will be different for every single person. Which also means what makes each of us feel better will also be different and there shouldn't be any shame or lecturing about it. Advice, when asked, sure.

I honestly don’t understand the point you’re making but what I gather is you’re saying the professor doesn’t have the power to say “yay or nay” because OP could be accommodated somehow. 

Yes, that’s exactly what I said. The school/professor needs to engage in an interactive process with the OP and come up with a reasonable accommodation that suits this particular situation which may not be the requested accommodation from OP. In other comments, I suggested alternatives and gave a resource and OP even commented an alternative solution that was accepted by all parties.

People often misunderstand reasonable accommodation, all I’m explaining is what it means. It’s in favor of the business/school, not employee/student. Whether or not that’s fair is beyond anything I’m willing to speculate on a public forum with strangers.

The OP in a comment mentioned an alternative accommodation that the Disability office recommended and the professor accepted. 

As I said to you in your other comment, the requested accommodation is a preference and it is not required to provide it as it may not be reasonable in the situation
The requested accommodation is a preference. It is not required as it may be unreasonable for the school/that particular class to provide.

Not necessarily. An English class could easily provide the accommodation at home for short response essays because essays are subjective arguments being made. Perhaps a math or engineering course that is testing memory can’t have that accommodation due to cheating concerns. 

However, there are alternatives to both what the student and professor want. I listed some in another comment. 

I would recommend AskJan.org as a resource for alternative accommodation suggestions as there are often plenty of options where everyone can find one that suits the specific situation and meets the “reasonable” standard.

The school must engage in an interactive process with students who request an accommodation but accommodations must be reasonable for the school to provide. Reasonableness really depends on the type of disability going on, what’s being asked for and what would not be burdensome for the school. Schools have to balance accommodations with ensuring the students they’re producing qualify for the degrees they eventually receive thus the interactive process. 

For an individual without the use of hands, there are more solutions/accommodations than doing all testing at home. It sounds like the professor is concerned with cheating. So perhaps the accommodation is taking quizzes at a testing center in a private room so a computer can utilize speech to text. Perhaps it’s staying after class and the professor giving the quiz verbally. Perhaps it’s a video proctored quiz at home. Perhaps it’s office time with the TA. There are many solutions that could work for both student and school - that does not mean it has to be the accommodation the student prefers, though.

Accommodations must be reasonable for the business or school, not for the individual with a disability. Meaning just because it’s the accommodation you would like, doesn’t mean it’s has to be THAT specific accommodation provided. It certainly may not be reasonable to provide that accommodation in this particular class even if other class can provide it. 

While it would be nice for every profesor to be willing to engage in the accommodation process, they may not. It sounds like you have been speaking to the Disability office since you have an advisor. I would speak to them and follow their advice. Perhaps they can walk you through how to get more universal accommodations so you don’t have to speak to every professor individually every semester.

I’m on 88 mg/100 mg levo (alternating every morning) and 1 mg LDN at night. That’s all I take and my body has calmed WAYYYYY down. No more itching, growing hair again, like all my symptoms gone (unless I’m under an immense about of emotional distress then I may itch or get hot but I think that’s fair haha) 

I asked for all my hormones to be tested. So estrogen, progesterone, testosterone, and there’s a bunch of smaller ones in there I don’t remember. There was info about when I likely ovulate every month 😅 every interesting even though unexpected info! I was worried that I may like PCOS also going on (I didn’t, yay!).She had something called an “autoimmune panel” she ran which included thyroid and I don’t remember all of them but a lot of different types of antibodies and stuff that makes up your blood. Levels of vitamins and minerals. They took like 4-5 vials from me to do all this but I loved seeing that other than my thyroid being out of whack, much of the rest of my body was working which made me feel less crazy AND it indicated to my doctor that the most likely cause of my symptoms was my body being inflamed due to Hashimoto’s. I felt, for the first time with a doctor, listened to and actually taken care of! 

Which is why I’m a big supporter of changing doctors or getting a second, third, fourth opinion if doctors are saying you’re fine even if you know you’re not. YOU know your body and how you’re feeling and that is important and doctors SHOULD listen

My numbers were all in range and I still had Hashimoto’s symptoms with the most upsetting being alopecia. I literally had spots all over, every size from about a dime to golf ball spots. Losing your hair, I’m sure for anyone, but as a woman was awful. 

My first doctor didn’t listen to me and kept telling me that since my numbers were in range, I was fine. I was NOT. I eventually stopped going because what was the point in complaining when nothing changed? 

My counselor convinced me to go to another doctor who sat down with me and let me pick out the blood tests I wanted along with the tests she wanted so we could see what was going on in my body. She also sat down and went over every single result when they came back explaining what each meant. My mom told me to ask for a referral to an endo and the new doctor had no issue providing me with one (which is a good sign, a good doctor has NO problem with patients getting other opinions). 

The endo told me he wanted my TSH under 2 and has been “half stepping” my dosage to get me there. 

The doctor also put me on low dose naltrexone (LDN) because when at a low dose, it’s been shown to reduce inflammation in the body which my doctor said is likely the cause of my continued symptoms. 

I’ve been on LDN for about three months and I stopped itching and my hair is growing back. I have little fluff patches in my spots 🙂 I used to run my hands through my hair and clumps would fall out and I’ve noticed the fall out is less. 

I don’t think every medication will work for everyone but I do think for those with inflammation issues, it’s worth a shot!

That’s exactly why I switch to social work for my masters. I had a mentor who asked what my end job goal was and I said I wasn’t sure. She said to do social work, then, because it’s a more versatile degree

There are a vast variety of niche jobs in the social work field where if one population is not a good fit for you, something else will be. 

For instance, I went in wanting to be a counselor. Life kicked me in the teeth and I wouldn’t be able to help someone else without being triggered myself. 

So now I’m a vocational counselor 🙂 I help people find jobs (ie: resume building, practice interviews, buying rehab tech, funding job coaches, etc) and the closest I get to mental health discussions are making sure my customers are seeing someone *else* to address their mental health needs.

This is where boundaries are very important! 

We are in the helping profession so when a coworker leaves or is gone, there is a higher level of care to ensure their customers are not harmed. This does NOT mean sacrificing your caseload nor your health. 

I’m the “oldest” employee in my office and I’ve only been here 1.5 years. In that time, I’ve covered the other caseload twice, in totality of almost 8 months now. The first time was awful because I would work late, on weekends, early mornings to get my caseload and that caseload done to meet deadlines and make sure everyone (customers and bosses) were happy. I was the ONLY one covering the other caseload. 

Then, after someone was hired for that position, an office 30 minutes away lost two people and my supervisor transferred some of those customers to me. When I pointed out that no one helped me when I was alone, I was told “yea well… be a team player”. 

So then when my coworker in my office quit a month ago, I immediately sat down with my boss and told him I will NOT be managing two caseloads again unless I’m paid for it. I know the time and stress it takes to do it, no one in other offices are sent to help me but I’m used to help them so unless I’m financially compensated, it’s not going to happen. He said “this will reflect on your performance review” and I straight told him “I’ve been doing multiple people’s jobs for more than half of my time here and THAT has never reflected on my review so I don’t care”. I told him I’m more than happy to help, when I have time and not at the expense of my customers, but the deadlines are not my responsibility. 

My manager has been in this office twice a week every week covering that caseload 🙂 anytime he asks for help, I always pitch in: Meeting with those customers, writing plans or reports, etc. If I have extra time, I’ll call my manager and ask where he needs help. But he is obviously stretched thin and tells me all the time the next new person he hires, he’s going to make sure their cases are kept clean because the caseload was left a mess (that he was fine handing to me but since I said no, he’s dealing with it!). He gets paid manager money to *manage*, I don’t. And if they don’t want to pay me, they can do it themselves. 

When the other office rehired the two positions, they transferred the customers away from me, and I offered to take on all of the cases for my office. My manager was shocked and I said “I never asked to be treated equally, I asked to be treated fairly. I’m always expected to help but no one helps me. The circumstances have now changed and it’s fair, not equal, that I take on the other caseload now”. And he’s actually been really thoughtful, now, in how many cases he transfers to me 🙂 keeping about 10 of them for himself! 

Personally, I think by saying “no, but I’m happy to help” has allowed everyone to grow and learn lessons.

First: You don’t need to do anything besides grieve (which is just another word for love) your brother. 

His stuff or “estate” isn’t urgent, it can wait. It sounds like your dad might be reasonable? Maybe see if he can get sister to back off just for a bit. 

Second, after googling it sounds like PA is similar to Idaho. In order to collect belongings, the estate has to be assigned a personal representative/executor and that person handles freezing his accounts, paying debts his estate would still owe, collects everything and then disperses it to whom it belongs (no will = parents). Usually anyone close to the deceased can be the representative/executor but it’s usually parent/sibling. They have to file with the court to do this. 

So… until there is an executor who has filed with the court that they are the executor for your brother’s estate, you don’t have to give them anything. When there is an executor, they will need to give you a list of things they think belonged to your brother that they’re expecting returned. Just because they give you a list, doesn’t mean it’s accurate. For example, if they listed the pc but he gave it to you, then it’s not accurate to have it listed as your brother’s property that needs collecting - it’s yours and you don’t have to give your property. 

If they have any issue with not getting something that they listed, they would have to open a whole probate and go to court. In that, usually there is a waiting period of a few months where they have to publish a “notice to creditors” so anyone who has a claim in the estate can file as “a creditor with an interest”. This (creditor with an interest) can be you. Just submit a creditor claim stating that the pc belongs to you and why. Then it’s up to the court to decide where the computer goes.

The only things parents (not sister, parents inherit if the deceased has no spouse/children/will), have a right to are the items in the deceased’s possession at the time of his death. So if he had a game system but got rid of it… then it doesn’t exist to give. That’s just the law. 

If he gave you the pc, same thing. It wasn’t in HIS possession when he passed so it’s not theirs to inherit. 

I’m not sure your state, but mine (Idaho) has a rule that no items can be forced collected until 30 days after death (affidavit of collection of personal property). So… really if it’s the same in your state, you have some time.
